reason: Multiple independent authoritative sources provide rich, cross-verified details on Betelgeuse's scale, runaway trajectory, the 2019–2020 Great Dimming, and its impending supernova.
story: In late 2019, the colossal red supergiant Betelgeuse began mysteriously fading, plunging from one of the night sky's brightest beacons down to 21st place. The sudden drop sparked worldwide panic that the monster star was about to detonate into a catastrophic supernova. Betelgeuse is genuinely terrifying in scale: if placed at the center of our solar system, its blistering surface would swallow Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. Furthermore, it is a runaway star speeding through the interstellar medium at 30 kilometers per second, carving out a bow shock light-years wide. Yet astronomers reassured the public that Earth was completely safe. Even if Betelgeuse blew up today—blazing as bright as a half-Moon and remaining visible in broad daylight for months—its roughly 500-light-year distance shields our planet from harm. Hubble observations ultimately revealed the dimming was not a death rattle, but a titanic ejection of superhot plasma that chilled into an obscuring dust cloud.
angle: If the runaway supergiant Betelgeuse sat where our Sun is, it would swallow Earth and Mars—and when it explodes, it will shine as bright as a half-Moon in broad daylight for months.

claims.claim: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star located in the equatorial constellation of Orion.
Betelgeuse is typically one of the brightest visible stars in the night sky and the brightest star at near-infrared wavelengths.
If placed at the center of our solar system, Betelgeuse's surface would engulf the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.
Betelgeuse is a runaway star traveling through interstellar space at approximately 30 kilometers per second (about 18.6 miles per second).
Betelgeuse's motion through the interstellar medium produces a massive bow shock measuring roughly three to four light-years wide.
Betelgeuse was ejected from its birthplace in the stellar association that includes the stars in Orion's Belt.
Betelgeuse is estimated to be roughly 400 to 600 light-years distant from Earth.
Ancient Chinese astronomers recorded Betelgeuse as yellow, whereas Ptolemy described it three centuries later as orange or tawny.
Beginning in October 2019, Betelgeuse began dimming drastically in an episode known as the Great Dimming.
During the Great Dimming, Betelgeuse dropped from among the top 10 brightest stars in the night sky down to 21st place.
Villanova astronomers Richard Wasatonic and Edward Guinan, along with amateur Thomas Calderwood, tracked and alerted the astronomical community to the record dimming.
The historic fading sparked intense speculation among the media and public that Betelgeuse was on the verge of exploding as a supernova.
Hubble Space Telescope observations indicated the dimming was caused by an enormous ejection of superhot plasma that cooled to form an obscuring dust cloud.
Astronomers estimate that Betelgeuse will end its life in a supernova explosion within roughly the next 100,000 years.
When Betelgeuse detonates as a supernova, it will shine approximately as bright as a half-Moon and remain visible during the day for months.
Life on Earth will be completely safe and unharmed when Betelgeuse explodes as a supernova.
The historical supernova SN 1054 in the Milky Way produced the Crab Nebula.
In 1980, astrophysicist Ken'ichi Nomoto predicted a distinct third category of stellar explosion called an electron-capture supernova.
Supernova SN 2018zd, located roughly 31 million light-years away in galaxy NGC 2146, provided astronomers with the first observational evidence of an electron-capture supernova.

disputed: Casting visible shadows on Earth: The prompt states the supernova would cast visible shadows on Earth for weeks, but none of the provided sources support this specific detail; a script should leave it out.

Exact distance to Betelgeuse: Estimates range across studies from ~410 light-years (125 pc) up to over 700 light-years, with S4 citing 640 ly and S3 quoting 548 ly. A script should state a general range of 400 to 600 light-years.

Bow shock size: S1 and S3 state the bow shock is roughly four light-years wide, while S4 states it is about three light-years in diameter. A script should phrase it as 'three to four light-years across'.

Cause of the Great Dimming: While Hubble observations suggest dust formed by a surface mass ejection, S1 and S6 note submillimetre studies and alternative models suggesting large photospheric starspots or cool patches. A script should attribute the dust cloud model to Hubble studies while noting ongoing scientific discussion.

Etymology of the name Betelgeuse: S1 describes the derivation from Arabic 'Yad al-Jawzā’' meaning 'hand of Orion', whereas S3 cites 'Ibṭ al-Jauzā’' meaning 'armpit of Orion'. A script should treat these as conflicting translations or leave the etymology out.
